family: Psittaculidae (Old World parrots; lorikeets and lories)
overview: The rainbow lorikeet is a small, fast, very bright parrot with a blue head, a green back, a blazing orange chest and a red beak. Noisy flocks zip between flowering trees along the east coast of Australia, screeching as they fly, and then chatter non-stop while they feed. Instead of cracking seeds like most parrots, lorikeets lap up nectar and pollen with a brush-tipped tongue. They are one of the most often seen birds in Australia and are common in city gardens.

deep_dive.habitat: Anywhere with flowering or fruiting trees: rainforest, coastal scrub, eucalypt woodland, parks, gardens and street trees. They follow the flowering of eucalypts, grevilleas, bottlebrushes and other nectar plants, and gather in big communal roosts at dusk.
deep_dive.range: The east and south-east of mainland Australia, from Cape York down the coast through New South Wales and Victoria to south-eastern South Australia. Introduced and now established around Perth (since the 1960s) and in Tasmania; an illegal release in Auckland was later removed. The IOC list now treats the coconut lorikeet (T. haematodus, New Guinea and islands) and the red-collared lorikeet (T. rubritorquis, northern Australia) as separate species. Two subspecies: moluccanus (east and south-east) and septentrionalis (Cape York).
deep_dive.behaviour: Lives in pairs inside larger flocks. Flocks fly fast and direct, screeching, and can be aggressive at feeders and around nest hollows, pushing out other hollow-nesting birds. Pairs stay together for a long time. They nest in tree hollows on chewed wood; both parents prepare the hollow and feed the young, but only the female incubates the one to three eggs. In parks many birds are tame enough to be hand-fed.
deep_dive.voice: Very noisy. Flight calls are sharp, rolling screeches given over and over; perched and feeding birds keep up a constant, shrill chattering and twittering, and pairs swap soft contact notes. Alarm calls are harsh, rapid screeches. In our recordings the calls have bright harmonic stacks with fundamentals of roughly 0.8-4 kHz (most around 2-3.5 kHz) and energy between about 2 and 8 kHz, higher and more tonal than the cockatoo's screech.
deep_dive.anatomy: A parrot (order Psittaciformes), not a songbird. The parrot syrinx sits at the base of the windpipe with a pair of thin lateral tympaniform membranes as a single sound source, moved by two small muscles inside the syrinx. Parrots then shape the sound with their thick, movable tongue, beak opening and windpipe length, which shift the vocal-tract resonances (studied in monk parakeets). The lorikeet's tongue ends in a brush of fine papillae for gathering pollen and nectar. The beak is small, hooked and coral red; young birds have a dark beak that turns orange-red as they grow. (These are parrot-wide findings, not lorikeet-specific studies.)
